entities.name: Plautius Quintillus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Plautius Quintillus, a Roman senator active in the mid-to-late 2nd century CE, achieved prominence primarily through his strategic marriage to Ceionia Fabia, the sister of Emperor Lucius Verus. This marital alliance, forged likely in the 160s CE, integrated Quintillus into the highest echelons of the Antonine dynasty, a period renowned for its relative stability and the rule of the 'Five Good Emperors.' His career epitomizes the path of a senatorial aristocrat whose influence was often more a function of familial connections and inherited status than individual, groundbreaking achievements, though his holding of the consulship marked him as a successful member of the Roman elite.

Quintillus's most notable documented achievement was his tenure as consul in 177 CE, an office he shared with Marcus Aurelius's son, Commodus, who was then co-emperor. This appointment placed him at the heart of Roman governance during a critical juncture, as Marcus Aurelius was heavily involved in the Marcomannic Wars on the northern frontier. While specific details of his actions as consul or any subsequent provincial commands are not extensively recorded in surviving historical sources, his very appointment signifies his trusted position within the imperial administration and his family's continued standing in Roman society.

The legacy of Plautius Quintillus is less about specific policy or military victories and more about the continuity of the Roman aristocratic system and the power of matrimonial alliances in maintaining the social and political fabric of the Empire. His family, through his marriage, gained direct lineage to emperors, ensuring their status and influence for at least another generation. Such connections were vital for stability, but also contributed to the consolidation of power within a narrow elite, shaping the future political landscape of Rome.
